To politely ask for information in the street.
To use the imperative: tourne, tournez, tournons.
To describe position: à gauche de, en face de, entre, devant…
To conjugate the verb VENIR and say where you come from.
To use ordinal numbers: premier, deuxième, troisième.
On Saturday evening Julien is playing the piano in a small venue in the Croix-Rousse district. Ioana has come out of the metro but can’t find the way. She asks a passer-by.
Excuse me, madam. I’m looking for the concert venue “Le Piano Rouge”. Is it far?
No, it’s very close! Can you see the square over there?
Yes, the one with the fountain?
That’s it. Cross the square, then take the second street on the right.
The second on the right… OK.
Carry straight on to the traffic lights. At the lights, turn left.
And where exactly is the venue?
It’s between a chemist’s and a bakery, opposite the church.
Thank you very much! You’re very kind.
You’re welcome. You’re not French, are you? Where are you from?
I’m from Romania. I’ve been living in Lyon for a month.
(Ten minutes later) Ioana! You came! Come on, come in, the concert’s starting!
Sorry, I’m a bit late. The streets in Croix-Rousse go uphill a lot!
OIN is read as a nasal “wẽ”: loin = “lwẽ”, coin = “kwẽ”, point = “pwẽ”.
Gauche = “gohsh” (AU = o, CH = sh). Droite = “drwat” (OI = wa, you hear the t because an -e follows).
VENIR has the nasal “yẽ” in the singular: je viens = “vyẽ”. In the plural it changes: ils viennent = “vyen”, no nasal.
Derrière = “deh-RYER”, deuxième = “duh-ZYEM”, troisième = “trwa-ZYEM”. The e with a grave accent is open.
The imperative is said in a firm, falling voice: “Tournez à gauche.” ↘ With “s’il vous plaît” it sounds softer.
1. How to ask for information in the street
Always start with “Excusez-moi” or “Pardon”, plus “madame / monsieur”. Then ask in one of these ways:
Excuse me, is the station far? (spoken)
I’m looking for the chemist’s, please.
How do I get to Place Bellecour, please?
If you don’t understand, say: “Pardon, vous pouvez répéter, s’il vous plaît ? Plus lentement ?” (Could you repeat that, please? More slowly?).
The French imperative has three forms: for “tu”, for “vous” and for “nous” (= let’s…). It comes from the present tense, WITHOUT the pronoun.
Careful: with -er verbs, the “tu” form LOSES its -s: “tu tournes” → “Tourne !”, “tu vas” → “Va !”. With other verbs the s stays: “tu prends” → “Prends !”, “tu viens” → “Viens !”.
Negative: ne + verb + pas: “Ne tournez pas à droite !” (Don’t turn right!).
3. Where it is: prepositions of place
entre la poste et le café
Prepositions with “de” contract: “à côté DU musée” (de + le), “près DES magasins” (de + les), but “à côté DE LA banque”. “Devant” and “derrière” have NO “de”: “devant le musée”.
Where you come from: venir DE + city, venir DE / D’ + feminine country, venir DU + masculine country, venir DES + plural.
She comes from France / from Italy.
We come from the United States.
“Revenir” (to come back) and “devenir” (to become) are conjugated the same way.
“Depuis” = “for / since”: “J’habite à Lyon depuis un mois” = “I’ve been living in Lyon for a month”. Careful: French uses the PRESENT tense here, not the present perfect.
Ordinals are formed by adding -ième to the number. Only “premier” is irregular.
Floors: “le rez-de-chaussée” = the ground floor, “le premier étage” = the first floor (one level above the ground floor, as in British English, not American).
